Short-Term Load Forecasting in an AMI Distribution Network: A Benchmark of Statistical, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Foundation Models

A reproducible one-step-ahead benchmark across SARIMA/SARIMAX, XGBoost, LSTM, Temporal Fusion Transformer, and TimesFM using 157.5 million smart-meter records from a real Norwegian distribution network.

Best R² — TimesFM zero-shot

Research problem

Can a pretrained time-series foundation model outperform target-trained statistical, machine-learning, and deep-learning forecasters under a rigorously aligned evaluation protocol?

Why this benchmark matters

AMI networks exhibit nested daily and weekly cycles, weather sensitivity, price effects, distributed generation, and abrupt changes in aggregate demand composition. Model comparisons are often confounded by inconsistent horizons, splits, features, or forecast timestamps.

Core design principle: every final prediction is aligned to the same 4,786-hour chronological holdout, without random shuffling across the temporal boundary.

Main finding

TimesFM achieved the best zero-shot result with RMSE 331.58, MAPE 2.36%, and R² 0.9905. It reduced RMSE by 15.76% relative to the strongest target-trained alternative, TFT with external variables.

Deeper result: external variables are not automatically beneficial. Their value depends on timing, stability, regularization, and the model's fusion mechanism.

Resumo em português

O estudo compara modelos estatísticos, machine learning, deep learning e um foundation model temporal na previsão horária de carga agregada de uma rede AMI. O TimesFM, utilizado sem ajuste fino, obteve o melhor desempenho. O resultado mais relevante, porém, é que preço e clima melhoraram XGBoost e TFT, mas degradaram SARIMAX, LSTM e o híbrido TimesFM–Ridge. Isso evidencia que a arquitetura de fusão das covariáveis é tão importante quanto a seleção das variáveis.

Distribution-network dataset

Real medium- and low-voltage radials near Porsgrunn, Norway, with anonymized AMI measurements, spot prices, weather observations, and network models.

Observation space

  • Period: 1 January 2022 to 30 September 2024.
  • Resolution: hourly.
  • Consumers: approximately 6.8 thousand.
  • Raw AMI rows: 157,538,434.
  • Model-ready observations: 23,928 after the 168-hour lag.
y_t = Σᵢ₌₁ᴺᵗ (Pᵒᵘᵗᵢ,ₜ − Pⁱⁿᵢ,ₜ)

Hourly net active consumption is the sum of active power out minus active power in across all meters observed at hour t.

Predictor architecture

Endogenous history

Lags at 1, 24, and 168 hours; rolling means over 3 and 24 hours; and a 24-hour rolling standard deviation.

lag 1hlag 24hlag 168hrolling 3hrolling 24h

Calendar variables

Hour, weekday, month, weekend status, and cyclical sine–cosine encodings for hour and weekday.

hourweekdaymonthsin/cos

External variables

Regional spot price and eight meteorological fields: temperature, humidity, cloud cover, precipitation probability, pressure, solar energy, solar radiation, and wind speed.

pricetemperaturehumiditysolarwind

Experimental methodology

A traceable pipeline preserves temporal order, separates endogenous and external information, and compares all models on a common forecast index.

Forecasting objective

ŷₜ₊₁ = f(y₁:ₜ, x₁:ₜ₊₁)

The task is rolling one-step-ahead forecasting. Trained statistical models update state with each observed test value without refitting parameters.

Chronological holdout

The first 80% of the model-ready sequence — 19,142 hours — is used for training. The last 20% — 4,786 hours — is reserved for final evaluation, from 15 March 2024 at 14:00 to 30 September 2024 at 23:00.

No random shuffling is performed across the boundary.

Stationarity and seasonality

The ADF test rejects the unit-root null for both the complete model-ready series and the training series, so the nonseasonal differencing order is fixed at d = 0. This does not remove the visible daily seasonality.

ADF complete: p = 0.00499ADF train: p = 0.00956Seasonal period: 24h

Leakage-safe feature engineering

Every rolling statistic is shifted by one hour before computation, preventing the current target from entering its own predictor vector.

Operational caveat: the external variables used in the test interval are realized historical values aligned to the forecast hour, not origin-available weather and price forecasts.

Evaluation metrics

Scale-dependent

MAE = mean(|yₜ − ŷₜ|)
RMSE = √mean((yₜ − ŷₜ)²)

RMSE penalizes larger errors more strongly and is used for the principal ranking.

Percentage-based

MAPE · sMAPE · WAPE

Multiple percentage metrics are retained instead of converting MAPE into a misleading “accuracy” value.

Explained variation

R² = 1 − SSE / SST

R² is reported alongside direct error measures to show how closely each model tracks aggregate variation.

Model families

The benchmark spans increasingly expressive paradigms, from persistence rules and linear seasonal structure to learned nonlinear representations and zero-shot transfer.

TimesFM–Ridge residual hybrid

Because native TimesFM XReg required additional JAX dependencies, Ridge regression first models the standardized external variables; TimesFM then forecasts the residual series.

This is an explicit additive hybrid and should not be confused with native TimesFM XReg.

When external information helps — and when it harms

The same price and weather block produces opposite outcomes across model families, revealing a strong interaction between covariate dynamics and architecture.

Effect of external variables on RMSE

Negative values indicate improvement; positive values indicate degradation.

Beneficial fusion

XGBoost: RMSE improves by 5.73%. Tree partitions can effectively suppress weak variables.

TFT: RMSE improves by 3.82%. Variable selection and gating allow complementary signals to contribute without forcing equal importance.

Harmful fusion

SARIMAX: +85.98% RMSE. The model assumes a linear and temporally stable regressor response.

LSTM: +204.89% RMSE. Concatenated standardized inputs expose the recurrent sequence to distribution shifts or unstable dominance.

TimesFM–Ridge: +200.07% RMSE. The additive residual decomposition does not preserve zero-shot strengths.

XGBoost feature relevance

The one-hour lag dominates; temperature is the most influential external field.

Interpretation

The one-hour lag accounts for approximately 74.56% of feature importance, temperature for 14.96%, month for 6.42%, and hour for 2.22%. Each remaining external field contributes less than 0.3%.

Physical plausibility is not sufficient evidence that a variable will improve a particular estimator.
Ex-post setting: realized test-hour weather and price measure explanatory forecasting potential. Operational deployment requires origin-available forecasts and uncertainty propagation.

Discussion

The benchmark supports a focused conclusion: for this one-step aggregate AMI task, the zero-shot prior is more valuable than target-specific fitting of the tested alternatives.

Why did TimesFM lead?

The series contains regular daily and weekly structure with variable amplitude. A 14-day context exposes two weekly cycles and multiple daily transitions. Pretraining supplies a broad library of temporal motifs, allowing adaptation through context rather than target-specific parameter fitting.

What the result does mean

  • Zero-shot transfer is highly competitive for this aggregate network.
  • TimesFM is a strong cold-start, benchmark, fallback, or ensemble component.
  • Foundation-model pretraining can outweigh local fitting under a narrow one-step setting.

What the result does not mean

  • Foundation models do not universally dominate trained forecasters.
  • TFT may become preferable for reliable future covariates, probabilistic outputs, or joint multi-horizon training.
  • Feeder-level and customer-level series may be noisier, sparser, and less transferable.

Operational model strategy

1 · Baseline

t−1

Use one-hour persistence as a non-negotiable operational reference.

2 · Compact learner

XGBoost

Prioritize interpretability, conventional retraining, and a small deployment footprint.

3 · Rich fusion

TFT

Use when future covariates, probabilistic outputs, or multi-horizon requirements justify complexity.

4 · Transfer baseline

TimesFM

Use for high-accuracy cold starts, limited tuning time, fallback, or ensemble construction.

Threats to validity

Single network and aggregation level

Results concern one aggregated active-net-consumption series.

Single chronological holdout

The long test interval does not quantify seasonal or yearly variation across multiple origins.

One-step horizon

Conclusions may change for day-ahead and multi-day forecasts.

Realized covariates

Operational forecasts must replace historical test-hour observations with origin-available forecasts.

Optimization and random seeds

Deep models were not subjected to exhaustive nested tuning; one principal seed was used.

SARIMA convergence

The lowest-AIC univariate candidate did not report optimizer convergence.

No formal paired significance test

Diebold–Mariano tests or block-bootstrap confidence intervals remain future work.

Pretraining provenance

Exact foundation-model corpus composition may not be fully observable; overlap cannot be independently excluded.

Reproducibility

The executed notebook stores the numerical outputs and figures used by the article. The dataset is publicly available under CC BY 4.0.

Five decisions that must be preserved

  1. Net load is activePowerOut - activePowerIn.
  2. Lag and rolling features are shifted before prediction.
  3. The split is chronological at 80%.
  4. Every model is evaluated on the same 4,786 timestamps.
  5. External-variable results use aligned historical covariates and must not be described as fully operational future-known forecasts.

Recorded computational observations

Seconds measured on the available CPU environment. XGBoost and TFT were not recorded on a strictly comparable end-to-end basis.

Engineering interpretation

TimesFM is the most accurate measured configuration but not the lightest in rolling CPU inference. Its 4,786 repeated forecast origins required 190.20 seconds in total.

XGBoost remains attractive when retraining speed, feature attribution, and deployment footprint are primary constraints. Batching multiple series or using an accelerator may improve TimesFM throughput.

The reported times are observations from one environment, not hardware-independent complexity results.
